notes: \cpara{Opens a mock film script: generals at a briefing, as in a disaster film.}
\cpara{``28 days ago'' points to the film \textsc{28 Days Later} (2002), in which a ``rage'' virus turns people into attackers. The next two questions ask whether these zombies are that kind.}

\cpara{Gives the philosophers' definition. Chalmers, in \textsc{The Conscious Mind} (1996, p.~95), set such zombies against Hollywood's, which ``tend to have significant functional impairments,'' and added: ``(Perhaps it is not surprising that phenomenal zombies have not been popular in Hollywood, as there would be obvious problems with their depiction.)''}
\cpara{Shows the problem of depiction: ``now'' looks just like ``two weeks ago,'' because by definition nothing observable has changed.}
\cpara{The ``epiphenomenal virus'': a cause with no observable effects. ``Dual properties of ordinary matter'' describes property dualism, the view discussed in ``Zombies! Zombies?''.}
\cpara{A joke on the same premise: a list of epiphenomena observed would be a list of events that left no trace.}

\cpara{Compresses an argument of ``Zombies! Zombies?'': on epiphenomenalism, our knowledge of our own consciousness cannot come from its effects. Chalmers's reply, quoted in that post, is that ``it is having the experiences that justifies the beliefs.'' The joke leaves the reply out, as a joke may.}
\cpara{An epiphenomenal cure would have no effects, so placebos fail because they have some. The homeopath and the Taoists, who ``refuse to do anything,'' are two more jokes on the same premise.}
\cpara{Shows Chalmers as a patient, whose reports about his own consciousness no longer count.}
\cpara{The character anticipates the objection: a zombie would say the same.}
\cpara{Matches Richard Chappell's comment, quoted in ``Zombie Responses,'' that zombie Chalmers's ``utterances are meaningless.''}

\cpara{Accurate to Chalmers's view: ``it is unlikely that zombies are naturally possible. In the real world, it is likely that any replica of me would be conscious'' (\textsc{The Conscious Mind}, p.~96).}

\cpara{The cut leaves the character without an answer. Chalmers's answer is that the laws linking physical states to experience, which Chalmers calls psychophysical and the author calls ``bridging laws,'' hold in our world; ``Zombies! Zombies?'' reports it. The police badge in the next scene alludes to those laws.}
\cpara{``Bridging Law Enforcement Agency'': a pun on the bridging laws.}
\cpara{The police recite the definition as a warning: the zombies are ``identical to humans on the atomic level. But they're not human.''}
\cpara{Brings in Daniel Dennett, author of ``The Unimagined Preposterousness of Zombies,'' as an action hero in black leather.}
\cpara{Dennett argues against qualia, as philosophers define them, in ``Quining Qualia'' (1988; summary from Wikipedia, ``Qualia'').}
\cpara{The joke turns on the zombie hypothesis itself: zombies and humans make the same claims, so claims cannot sort them, and a denial fits neither.}
\cpara{Slapstick: the philosopher disarms both officers.}
\cpara{A joke on materialism, Dennett's side of the debate.}
\cpara{Reverses the line ``There is no spoon'' from \textsc{The Matrix} (1999).}
\cpara{A pun on reductionism.}
\cpara{Reverses disaster-film lines: ``total normality,'' ``the middle of humanity.''}
\cpara{The zombies' reply mirrors the humans' charge. On the zombie hypothesis each side says the same things for the same reasons, which is the point of the zombie twin in ``Zombies! Zombies?''.}
\cpara{The ending puts the case in one line. Removing the film's picture and sound, like removing epiphenomenal consciousness, changes nothing that happens.}
\cpara{A photograph, which I could not see; the caption says it shows the author ``being attacked by zombie nurses at Penguicon.''}
\cpara{An anecdote from the convention. Penguicon, in Michigan, was founded to bring together science-fiction fans and Linux users (Wikipedia). The joke is the heckler's question about the prior.}
